My land here in Quzhou is about 15 mu. My family has farmed this ground for three generations. Everyone around me does winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same fields — that's just how it works here on the plain. The soil is sandy loam, the wells run deep, and I know the rhythm of it. I'm not going to change what I grow. The grain station in town still takes wheat and maize at a fixed price, and that gives me security. My brother tried cotton a few years back and had a rough time selling it. I'm not doing that.

For the wheat, I'll use the Jimai variety I've been buying from the county seed co-op — improved certified seed. It does well here and resists the rust disease we get some years. I till the field with the rotary tiller after maize harvest in late September, apply base fertilizer, then sow in early October. I irrigate before sowing to get good germination, again in late winter before the freeze breaks, and once more at jointing. Three times is what my father did, what I do. For maize, I plant straight into the stubble after wheat harvest in June — no tilling, saves diesel and time. Maize is straightforward; the summer rains usually cover most of what it needs. I'll spray once for corn borer if I see it.

Fertilizer I apply more or less what the village agronomist told me years ago. I use compound fertilizer as base and urea as topdress. I don't test the soil — nobody around here does.
